{
  "question_intent": "Competitive dynamics, market share, RWA efficiency, UK politics impact",
  "main_topics": ["Investment Bank capital", "Regulatory changes", "Competitive dynamics", "Market share", "RWA recycling", "UK politics", "Strategy", "UK banking environment", "Growth", "Risk management"],
  "answer_completeness": "Complete",
  "response_stance": "Direct",
  "evidence_level": "High",
  "contains_numeric_evidence": true,
  "contains_forward_guidance": true,
  "narrative_alignment": "Aligned",
  "question_quote": "And the second question was around U.K. politics, which I appreciate you might try to dodge. But I guess it wasn't that long ago that Barclays talked about the UK political backdrop being the best it's been in a long, long time. Presumably, that informed the renewed push into the UK, particularly on the corporate side. So if we do see a meaningful shift to the higher taxes, be that personal, corporate, banking taxes, whatever it might be, could that change the strategy?",
  "answer_quote": "So what Venkat was really getting at on the [Barclays Q126 Results] call was that if you go back over the last few quarters, it's not just in Q1 that we've seen a change in either capital or leverage deployed across the industry more broadly. It's actually been several quarters now. So probably more marked in the first quarter just because of the market environment that we saw in particular. So perhaps more of a step change there. So you're seeing both a seasonal step-up and you're also seeing, if you like, that volatility impact. But we've seen it sort of quarter in, quarter out for quite a few quarters now, and I'd encourage you to go back and look at that. It's certainly something that we are focused on. From our perspective, we still think that there's more to go. And our choice here is to run the IB in a very, very disciplined way. So we did put more RWAs into the IB in the quarter. And we felt we did that in an appropriate way. You can see that our Markets results in particular, are broadly in the pack, if you look at them in dollars. FICC, you have to recall, has got no commodities in it. So ex commodities, we think that's a good performance. Equities was right in the middle of the pack. And we did so while still increasing our revenue over RWA, went up to 8% in the quarter. We had one loss day and the VAR was flat. So across risk and across capital deployment, our choice is to be disciplined. Because fundamentally, our goal with this business is to get to a sustainably higher level of RoTE. So expect us to keep going down that route. We still think there's more to go on the optimisation of RWAs. Not least there's another year to go, because remember, at the beginning of the story, we said there was three years' worth of banking to work through. So we're only sort of two years and one quarter through that. So still a bit more to go there. And we continue to learn. And obviously, in this kind of environment, capital moves quickly. The velocity of capital goes up. So your risk management needs to be very good. That's where the discipline comes in. But we remain confident that we can continue to do this. And of course, much of the areas of growth that we are focused on, we'd either put capital into already or are inherently capital-light. And I'll just take you back to the sort of guidance that we gave you on the 10th of February [2026], we said that our market share would be broadly stable, and we are expected to see some growth in [Investment] Banking. Now [Investment] Banking, remember, is capital light. So we're already mindful of this environment when we give you the targets that we have. So expect RWAs to be broadly stable. Expect us to lean in and out depending on what the market opportunity is and to retain that very strict discipline, both around risk and around capital. Let me move to UK politics. So when we announced our strategy in 2024, that was a year in the making. So we had concluded before the change of government that it was the right thing to lean into the UK. And we believe that deeply for a couple of reasons. The first is that we believe the Bank should be rebalanced. The Investment Bank has the right waterfront, and therefore, our choice is to grow, particularly in the UK. That's a more stable source of returns for us, that's the highest returning part of the business. So that drove our choice, but also, a reflection as we look at universal banks across the globe, the really successful ones are very strong in their home market. And we felt that we needed more emphasis there. So it was driven by that. The political environment then changed and was then consistent with that. We would hope that whatever happens, the political environment is still geared towards growth. That's what the UK needs. It needs growth, it needs productivity. We believe that what we are doing is important as a part of that. And so we will continue that strategy. Of course, if the credit environment changed markedly, you would expect us to look at that, but the change in government alone would not be sufficient."
}
